title: Oncogenic modulation of MAPK signaling in leukemia via SPNS2-driven sphingolipid metabolism and membrane nanodomains remodeling
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Lipid metabolism rewiring is an essential determinant of cancer progression, yet the key metabolic checkpoints which govern this process remain poorly defined. Using functional genomics in a mouse model of acute myeloid leukemia (AML), we identify the sphingosine-1-phosphate transporter SPNS2 as a critical sphingolipid checkpoint protein which modulates leukemia progression. SPNS2 expression is regulated by MYC and progressively declines during AML differentiation, highlighting its tumor-suppressive role in a subset of Core Binding Factor AMLs. By integrating steady-state and serine isotope-tracing lipidomics, RNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and high-resolution microscopy, with gain- and loss-of-function approaches, we show that SPNS2 modulation rewires sphingolipid metabolism by modifying sphingomyelin abundance. This remodeling alters membrane nanodomain organization, active RAS localization, and MAPK signaling. Exogenous reintroduction of SPNS2 decreases sphingomyelin levels, disrupts nanodomain organization, and limits leukemic progression in various AML mouse models. We further reveal in a cohort of patients with AML that low SPNS2 expression is associated with increased sensitivity to MAPK pathway inhibition, and demonstrate functionally in vivo that SPNS2 silencing sensitizes AML cells to MEK1/2 inhibition. Collectively, our data reveal a mechanism by which sphingolipid transport dynamics intersect with oncogenic signaling to control cancer progression.

title: Cryo-EM reveals major proteolysis independent substrate rearrangements in a complement C5 convertase surrogate complex(es)
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Despite extensive structural analysis of the complement cascade, a detailed understanding of complement C5 activation is lacking. Here we show using cryo-EM that C5 in complex with the CVFBb surrogate convertase undergoes a proteolysis independent two-step rearrangement to a C5* conformation that enables the C5 scissile bond to reach the catalytic site of the Bb protease. C5* can form a complex with C6 and initiate membrane attack complex formation without C5 cleavage. Moreover, we observe an unusual convertase conformation where Bb rotates 155° relative to CVFBb in the putative Michaelis complex. This work demonstrates that the C5* conformation is functionally relevant and can help rationalize the mode of action for known C5 inhibitors, and we propose that large Bb rotations may allow the endogenous surface bound C5 convertases to cleave in trans C5 bound to a neighboring C3b molecule, presenting a refined model of C5 cleavage in vivo.

title: Genetic integration reveals causal effects of chromatin accessibility on nucleosome positioning across diverse muscle cells
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Cell type-specific chromatin accessibility QTL (caQTL) mapping is a promising approach to understand genetic control of chromatin landscapes and identify regulatory mechanisms underlying GWAS associations. However, current caQTL studies lack resolution and do not distinguish nucleosome-free regions (NFR) from positioned nucleosomes. Here, we leverage statistical modeling of fragment position and length to decompose ATAC-seq profiles into NFRs and phased nucleosomes. With single nucleus (sn)ATAC-seq from 281 human muscle biopsies, we map cell type-specific genetic effects on NFRs (76,027 nfrQTLs) and nucleosome occupancy (24,623 nucQTLs) across skeletal muscle cell types. Colocalization and causal inference analyses identify 1,528 instances where nfrQTLs have likely causal effects on adjacent nucleosome positioning, supporting a causal relationship in shaping chromatin profiles. Hundreds of nfrQTLs colocalize with GWAS signals for muscle-related traits, including grip strength, atrial fibrillation, and fasting insulin, and the majority of colocalizing signals mapped to credible sets overlapping the corresponding nfrPeak. This approach adds mechanistic insights for how variants underlying skeletal muscle caQTLs and GWAS signals exert their cis regulatory effects by initially modifying NFR accessibility and subsequently shaping broader chromatin landscapes, nucleosome positioning, gene expression, and ultimately higher-level traits and disease.

title: Coevolutionary constraints of Zika virus nonstructural protein 5 replication and interferon antagonism activities
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: The flavivirus nonstructural protein 5 performs multiple functions during infection, including RNA replication and type I interferon signaling antagonism. Although flavivirus NS5 proteins inhibit IFN signaling through distinct mechanisms, which suggests evolutionary flexibility, the evolutionary constraints for these activities to coexist within a single protein remain to be determined. Here, we map the Zika virus NS5 STAT2 antagonism determinants and compare them with replication constraints defined by deep mutational scanning. Antagonism and replication determinants extensively overlap, and no single amino acid substitution eliminates antagonism without impairing replication. Resolving these fitness landscapes in parallel identifies specific combinations of partially functional substitutions that retain replication capacity while markedly reducing antagonism. These viruses are profoundly attenuated in human STAT2 knock-in mice. Our results uncover a fundamental evolutionary constraint linking replication and immune evasion activities in NS5, highlight that STAT2 antagonism is essential for ZIKV pathogenesis and provide new avenues for attenuated ZIKV vaccines.

title: Genetic mechanisms underlying the associations between brain structure and mental health
source: Biological sciences : Nature Communications subject feeds
abstract: Brain-wide association studies have linked brain structure to complex mental health phenotypes, yet the genetic underpinnings of these effects remain largely unclear. Here, we leverage multimodal neuroimaging, behavioral and genetic data from the UK Biobank to develop an integrative framework combining brain-wide association studies and GWAS to elucidate how genetic variants affect the relationship between brain structure and mental health. Our multivariate brain-wide association study identifies two reproducible brain structural modes: a cerebellar-dominant mode and a cortical-dominant mode that explain individual differences in mental health measures. Using GWAS, we subsequently identify 30 and 15 independent significant variants respectively for each mode, indicating distinct genetic architectures with no signal overlap. Post-GWAS analyses indicate distinct biological pathways: the cerebellar-dominant mode is enriched for genes involved in chromatin organization and epigenetic regulation, while the cortical-dominant mode is linked to neurotransmitter metabolism. Moreover, we identify shared genetic influences between the brain modes and both mental health and cognitive traits, as well as causal effects of the brain modes on these outcomes. We validate the framework in the independent HCP cohort, supporting the cross-cohort generalizability of the identified brain–behavior and genetic associations.
